title: How to Protect Your Family From Deepfakes
author: The Slow AI
summary: Using two recent cases — a deepfaked video of Australia's Prime Minister used to sell a crypto scam, and an engineering firm that lost roughly £19 million after every participant on a video call except one employee turned out to be an AI-generated deepfake — the piece argues that ordinary families, not just public figures or corporations, are now realistic targets for AI voice and video cloning fraud. It cites research showing three seconds of audio is enough to clone a voice, and that even trained listeners only catch deepfaked speech about 73 percent of the time in isolation, with familiarization training barely improving detection. The piece's core contribution is five concrete household defenses: agreeing on a family safe word that is spoken aloud and never written down or texted; always hanging up and calling back on a number already saved in the phone rather than one supplied by the caller; refusing to move money on the first call regardless of manufactured urgency; briefing the family members most likely to be targeted (typically parents) on the scam pattern in advance; and reporting incidents immediately, since the odds of recovering a wrongly sent payment fall by the hour.
points: The claim that even trained listeners only detect deepfaked speech about 73% of the time in isolation, with familiarization adding under four percentage points, argues that human vigilance alone is an inadequate defense, making structural precautions (safe words, callback protocols) necessary rather than optional.

The Arup case (every participant on a video call except one employee was a deepfake, resulting in fifteen transfers and roughly £19 million in unrecovered losses) demonstrates that even sophisticated, security-conscious organizations are vulnerable, undercutting the assumption that competence alone protects against this fraud.

The specific instruction that a family safe word must be 'chosen out loud, never written down, never texted' targets the exact vulnerability deepfake scams exploit — any digital record of the phrase could itself be harvested and used by an attacker.

Framing urgency itself as 'the tell' — since every version of the scam manufactures a reason payment must happen immediately — gives families a single, generalizable heuristic (delay any request for money by at least an hour) that applies across the different specific scam scenarios described.
quotes: ASIC, Australia's financial regulator, issued a warning on 17 August. Scammers had taken real footage of Anthony Albanese and grafted a synthetic voice onto it, pitching a fake trading platform called AUFIRST as a government 'tax dividend.'
Three seconds of audio is enough to clone a voice, and Microsoft proved it in 2023. Yours is in a voicemail greeting, a work video, a wedding speech somebody posted, a TikTok your kid tagged you in.

And if you think competence protects you, the British engineering firm Arup lost HK$200 million, about £19 million, to a video call. Every person on that call except him was a deepfake. He made fifteen transfers. None of the money has been recovered.

Researchers at UCL played 529 people a mix of real and deepfaked speech, in English and Mandarin. Hearing a clip on its own, with nothing to compare it against, listeners caught the fakes 73% of the time. Training them barely moved it: familiarisation added under four percentage points.
Agree a family safe word. This is Starling Bank's Safe Phrases idea, and it is the cheapest defence there is. One word or a short phrase, chosen out loud, never written down, never texted.

No money moves on the first call. Urgency is the tell. Every version of this scam, from the fake son to the fake CFO, manufactures a reason it must happen now: the train leaves, the deal closes, the bail hearing is in an hour.
